cards.title: Nash equilibria in concurrent terminal-reward games
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Does every finite two-player concurrent game with nonnegative terminal rewards admit an exact Nash equilibrium in randomized strategies that depend on the history of visited states? Play may continue forever, in which case both players receive zero. Existence is required from every specified initial state; strategies may use unbounded memory.
cards.why: Tests whether nonnegative eventual rewards suffice for exact strategic stability in the simplest concurrent infinite-duration setting. It separates the existence of stable behavior from restrictions on memory, computation or approximate incentives.
cards.status_note: Read the original model, strategies, payoff definition, counterexample and concluding question; checked the full 2016 follow-up, including its explicit open-status passage and Definition 6. Later-result searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution of this exact two-player nonnegative state-history target. Results for approximate equilibria or other information models were not treated as resolutions.

sentences: Two players act simultaneously in a finite state graph.
A terminal state pays each player a nonnegative reward once; infinite nonterminating play pays zero.
The question asks whether an exact Nash equilibrium always exists in randomized state-history strategies with unrestricted memory.
Negative terminal rewards already admit counterexamples.
A later existence theorem uses imprecise deviations and does not settle the exact question.

cards.definitions:
A game has a finite nonempty state set \(S\), a specified initial state \(s_0\), and two players \(i\in\{1,2\}\). At each state \(s\), player \(i\) has a finite nonempty action set \(A_i(s)\). Both players choose actions simultaneously. A deterministic transition function maps \((s,a_1,a_2)\) to the next state. There is no additional random transition mechanism.

Terminal states are absorbing: every legal action pair leaves their state unchanged. Each terminal state \(f\) has a fixed finite real reward \(r_i(f)\geq0\) for each player. A play that first reaches \(f\) gives player \(i\) the one-time payoff \(r_i(f)\). A play that never reaches a terminal state gives zero. There are no intermediate rewards, discounting or repeated payments after absorption. No promise of almost-sure termination is imposed.

A strategy \(\sigma_i\) assigns a probability distribution on \(A_i(s_t)\) to every finite visited-state history \(s_0s_1\cdots s_t\). At each round, actions are drawn independently for the two players according to these distributions. The strategy has access to state history, not the history of either player's chosen actions. This is the source's action-insensitive behavioral model, called “mixed strategies” there. It permits arbitrary history dependence and real probabilities; neither finite memory nor computability is required.

The transition rule and strategies induce a probability distribution on infinite plays. Let \(u_i(\sigma_1,\sigma_2;s_0)\) be the expected one-time payoff, including zero on nontermination. Rewards are bounded because the game is finite, so this expectation is well defined. A profile is an exact Nash equilibrium from \(s_0\) if
\[
u_i(\tau_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)\leq u_i(\sigma_i,\sigma_{-i};s_0)
\]
for both players and every alternative strategy \(\tau_i\) in the same state-history model. The other player's strategy stays fixed.

The question quantifies over every such finite game and initial state. It asks for an equilibrium against all permitted deviations, not merely stationary deviations, and does not require an equilibrium after every possible history as subgame perfection would. No payoff threshold, welfare guarantee or algorithm for constructing the profile is part of the target. Positive scaling of a player's rewards preserves the question, but adding a constant only at terminals need not: infinite plays still receive zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that an exact equilibrium exists for every game and initial state in the specified two-player, nonnegative, state-history model, or give a finite game in that model and prove that no permitted strategy profile is an exact equilibrium from its initial state. A failure of stationary or finite-memory equilibria alone is insufficient. Approximate equilibria and equilibria under imprecise deviations do not meet the exact criterion.

context_blocks.title: Finite states still allow infinite play
context_blocks.text: Nash’s theorem for finite normal-form games does not directly settle this setting. A finite state graph can generate arbitrarily long histories, and never reaching a terminal can change the payoff discontinuously.

context_blocks.title: Nonnegative rewards are essential
context_blocks.text: The source gives a two-player counterexample when negative terminal rewards are allowed. Its conclusion explains why an earlier claimed nonnegative counterexample does not work: shifting terminal rewards changes their comparison with nontermination.

context_blocks.title: The later relaxation does not settle exact existence
context_blocks.text: The 2016 paper still lists exact existence for two players as open, even for binary terminal rewards. It proves existence under imprecise deviations, where a deviation must remain profitable throughout a neighborhood to count. This is distinct from both exact Nash equilibrium and the usual tolerance on payoff improvement.

cards.context:
Nash’s theorem for finite normal-form games does not directly settle this setting. A finite state graph can generate arbitrarily long histories, and never reaching a terminal can change the payoff discontinuously.

The source gives a two-player counterexample when negative terminal rewards are allowed. Its conclusion explains why an earlier claimed nonnegative counterexample does not work: shifting terminal rewards changes their comparison with nontermination.

The 2016 paper still lists exact existence for two players as open, even for binary terminal rewards. It proves existence under imprecise deviations, where a deviation must remain profitable throughout a neighborhood to count. This is distinct from both exact Nash equilibrium and the usual tolerance on payoff improvement.
